12	
13	Terms used below:
14	
15	- **The script** is `packs/repo-governance/.apm/skills/navigate-decisions/scripts/navigate_decisions.py`. **The skill file** is the `SKILL.md` beside its `scripts/` directory.
16	- **The health command** is `python3 <the script> health --root <repository> [--today YYYY-MM-DD]`. **The health result** is the JSON it prints on stdout.
17	- **Today** is the `--today` value, or the current date in UTC when it is absent.
18	- **An admitted record** is one the script's existing corpus admission returns. Its **status word** is the first whitespace-separated word of its lifecycle value. **An accepted record** has status word `Accepted`. **A superseded ADR** is an admitted ADR with status word `Superseded`. **Its successors** are the ADR and RFC identifiers in its `Superseded by` header field.
19	- **The header** of a record is the text after its H1 line and before its first line starting `## `.
20	- **Record lines** are the record's text split on `\n`, with one `\r` directly before each `\n` removed.
21	- **A section** of a record is the lines after a line equal to `## <name>` up to the next line starting `## `.
22	- **The trigger text** of an ADR is taken from the first line in its `Consequences` section that starts `**Revisit if:**` or `- **Revisit if:**`. Take the rest of that line, with one trailing HTML comment and surrounding whitespace removed.
23	  - When that rest is not empty, the trigger text is it, followed by each next line up to the first blank line or line starting `#`, `- **` or `**`.
24	  - When it is empty and the next line is blank, the trigger text is the lines after that blank line that start `- `, or start with a space or tab and are not blank, up to the first line that is neither.
25	  - When it is empty and the next line is not blank, the trigger text is the next lines up to the first blank line or line starting `#`, `- **` or `**`.
26	  - Lines are joined with one space.
27	  An ADR with no such line, or whose trigger text is empty, has no trigger.
28	- **A date mention** in a text is a match, not touching a letter, digit, `_` or `-` on either side, of one of these forms. Matches are taken left to right; where several start at the same place the longest wins, and a match that overlaps an earlier one is not taken, so `5 October 2026` is one mention. Each form names a last day:
29	  - `YYYY-MM-DD`, a real calendar date: that day;
30	  - `YYYY-MM`, month 01 to 12: the last day of that month;
31	  - `<Month> D, YYYY` or `D <Month> YYYY`, with `<Month>` an English month name with a capital first letter, a real calendar date: that day;
32	  - `<Month> YYYY`: the last day of that month;
33	  - `Q1 YYYY` to `Q4 YYYY`: the last day of that quarter;
34	  - a bare year from `1900` to `2099`: 31 December of that year.
35	
36	  A date mention **has passed** when its last day is before today.
37	- **A version mention** in a text is a match of either form:
38	  - optionally one of `v`, `>=`, `<=`, `==`, `~=` or `^`, then two or more dot-separated digit runs, then an optional `+`, not preceded by a letter, digit, `_`, `.` or `-` and not followed by more letters or digits joined to it by `.`, `_` or `-`;
39	  - `v` followed by digits, not preceded by a letter, digit, `_`, `.` or `-` and not followed by a letter, digit, `_` or `.`.
40	- **The trigger class** of an accepted ADR is the first that applies:
41	  1. `due`: its trigger text holds a date mention that has passed;
42	  2. `version`: it holds a version mention;
43	  3. `scheduled`: it holds a date mention;
44	  4. `stable`: its trigger text, with one pair of wrapping backticks removed and casefolded, is `stable`, or starts with `stable` followed by a space, `—`, `-` or `:`;
45	  5. `judge`: any other trigger text. These are the "needs a person to judge" items;
46	  6. `none`: the ADR has no trigger.
47	- **A header citation** of a superseded ADR S by an accepted record R is a match of S's identifier as a whole word in R's header, where all of these hold:
48	  - R is not S and is not one of S's successors;
49	  - the match is not in R's `Supersedes` or `Supersedes in part` field;
50	  - R's header names none of S's successors as a whole word.
51	- **The signal text** of an accepted ADR is, for each line in its `Confirmation` section that starts with `**Signal`, `- **Signal` or the same after spaces, that line and the lines after it up to the next line, after leading spaces and a `- ` are removed, that starts `**Mode`, `**Signal` or `**Owner`.
52	- **A URI scheme** is, at the start of a text, an ASCII letter followed by one or more ASCII letters, digits, `+`, `-` or `.`, then `:`. A single letter before `:` is a drive letter, not a scheme.
53	- **A path candidate** comes from a backtick span or a Markdown link target in signal text:
54	  - a backtick span is the text between a pair of single backticks on one line. Remove a trailing `::` and everything after it, then a trailing `:` followed by digits, optionally `-` and digits. What is left is skipped when it starts with a URI scheme, so `cli.py:247` yields `cli.py` and `https://example.com/x` is skipped;
55	  - a link target is the text in `](…)` up to its first space. Targets that start with a URI scheme and targets starting `#` are skipped. Remove a `#` or `?` and everything after it;
56	  - the result is a path candidate when it is not empty, holds no whitespace and none of `<`, `>`, `*`, `?`, `[`, `]`, `{`, `}`, `$` or `|`, and either holds `/` or ends with `.` and one to five ASCII letters or digits.
57	- **The checked form** of a candidate is, for a backtick span, the candidate as written. For a link target, it is the target lexically joined to the ADR's directory and normalised, so `..` segments are resolved; a target that does not start with `/` and whose normalised form leaves the repository root is invalid.
58	- **A rooted candidate** is one that is invalid, or whose checked form's first `/`-separated segment equals the name of an entry directly under the repository root. A candidate that is not rooted is **unlocated**.
59	- **A signal item** is one ADR and one checked form: candidates with the same ADR and checked form are one item. Every count and list of candidates in the health result is of signal items, except where AC-0025 counts occurrences. A signal item is reported by its checked form, cleaned.
60	- **The lexical rule:** a candidate is invalid when its checked form starts with `/`, `~` or a drive letter and `:`, holds `\`, a NUL or any character of Unicode category `Cc`, `Cf`, `Zl`, `Zp`, `Co` or `Cs`, has a `.` or `..` segment, is longer than 160 code points, or has more than 32 `/`-separated segments. A backtick candidate with an empty segment, other than one trailing `/`, is also invalid.
61	- **The probe result** of a rooted candidate is one of:
62	  - `invalid`: it fails the lexical rule; or a component on its path is a symbolic link, a reparse point, or neither a regular file nor a directory; or its last component is a regular file with more than one hard link; or inspecting a component fails for any reason other than "does not exist", or the confinement helper refuses a directory on its path;
63	  - `missing`: not invalid, and inspecting some component reports that it does not exist, or a component before the last is a regular file;
64	  - `present`: any other rooted candidate.
65	- **Reported text** is a string the health result takes from record text: a trigger excerpt, a path candidate, a title, or a field value. Its **cleaned form** joins its lines with one space, removes every character of Unicode category `Cc`, `Cf`, `Zl`, `Zp`, `Co` or `Cs`, and cuts it to its first 160 code points, adding `…` when it cut. A rooted checked form that is not invalid is never cut, because the lexical rule makes any longer one invalid.
66

71	Each criterion compares the health result on the accuracy worktree, with `--today` set to the `today` value the hand check records, against the hand check.

74	- [ ] **AC-0031.** Every ADR the health result classes `judge` is classed `judge` in the hand check.
75	- [ ] **AC-0032.** The hand check lists no `due`, `version`, header-citation, `missing` or `invalid` item, and no accepted ADR without a `Confirmation` section, that the health result omits.

  - the result is a path candidate when it is not empty, holds no whitespace and none of `<`, `>`, `*`, `?`, `[`, `]`, `{`, `}`, `$` or `|`, and either holds `/` or ends with `.` and one to five ASCII letters or digits.
- **The checked form** of a candidate is, for a backtick span, the candidate as written. For a link target, it is the target lexically joined to the ADR's directory and normalised, so `..` segments are resolved; a target that does not start with `/` and whose normalised form leaves the repository root is invalid.
- **A rooted candidate** is one that is invalid, or whose checked form's first `/`-separated segment equals the name of an entry directly under the repository root. A candidate that is not rooted is **unlocated**.
- **A signal item** is one ADR and one checked form: candidates with the same ADR and checked form are one item. Every count and list of candidates in the health result is of signal items, except where AC-0025 counts occurrences. A signal item is reported by its checked form, cleaned.
- **The lexical rule:** a candidate is invalid when its checked form starts with `/`, `~` or a drive letter and `:`, holds `\`, a NUL or any character of Unicode category `Cc`, `Cf`, `Zl`, `Zp`, `Co` or `Cs`, has a `.` or `..` segment, is longer than 160 code points, or has more than 32 `/`-separated segments. A backtick candidate with an empty segment, other than one trailing `/`, is also invalid.
- **The probe result** of a rooted candidate is one of:
  - `invalid`: it fails the lexical rule; or a component on its path is a symbolic link, a reparse point, or neither a regular file nor a directory; or its last component is a regular file with more than one hard link; or inspecting a component fails for any reason other than "does not exist", or the confinement helper refuses a directory on its path;
  - `missing`: not invalid, and inspecting some component reports that it does not exist, or a component before the last is a regular file;
  - `present`: any other rooted candidate.
- **Reported text** is a string the health result takes from record text: a trigger excerpt, a path candidate, a title, or a field value. Its **cleaned form** joins its lines with one space, removes every character of Unicode category `Cc`, `Cf`, `Zl`, `Zp`, `Co` or `Cs`, and cuts it to its first 160 code points, adding `…` when it cut. A rooted checked form that is not invalid is never cut, because the lexical rule makes any longer one invalid.

## The criteria this record is compared against

### Accuracy on this repository

Each criterion compares the health result on the accuracy worktree, with `--today` set to the `today` value the hand check records, against the hand check.

- [ ] **AC-0030.** Every `due`, `version`, header-citation, `missing`, `invalid` and no-`Confirmation` item in the health result appears in the hand check with the same values.
- [ ] **AC-0031.** Every ADR the health result classes `judge` is classed `judge` in the hand check.
- [ ] **AC-0032.** The hand check lists no `due`, `version`, header-citation, `missing` or `invalid` item, and no accepted ADR without a `Confirmation` section, that the health result omits.
- [ ] **AC-0033.** The ledger records every reading disagreement with eugenelim's ruling, and none is ruled a defect in health.

1	# ADR-0076: Briefs persist; dispatch starts from specs
2	
3	- **Status:** Accepted
4	- **Date:** 2026-08-08
5	- **Areas:** shaping, workspace
6	- **Reversibility:** high
7	- **Decision-makers:** eugenelim
8	- **Supersedes:** none
9	- **Supersedes in part:** none
10	- **Superseded by:** none
11	- **Superseded in part:** ADR-0098 D1,D2; ADR-0092 D7
12	- **Related:** ADR-0009, ADR-0019, ADR-0033, ADR-0051,
13	  `work-intake-and-artifact-routing.md`; ADR-0078 records standalone intake
14	  and deterministic workspace indexing while preserving this ADR's
15	  persistent-brief and spec/plan-only dispatch rules
16	
17	## Decision summary
18	
19	- **Decision:** An accepted brief may remain Ready without specs; only selected
20	  delivery slices become spec/plan pairs, and agents may dispatch work only from
21	  structured workspace entries that reference those files.
22	- **Because:** a cold-start session needs a complete, reviewable contract and
23	  deterministic routing rather than requirements reconstructed from comments.
24	- **Applies to:** briefs, derived specs and plans, `workspace.toml`,
25	  `receive-brief`, `new-spec`, `workspace-status`, and `work-loop`.
26	- **Tradeoff accepted:** choosing work from a brief requires an explicit
27	  materialization step before execution.
28	- **Revisit if:** adopters need briefs themselves to be executable, or a
29	  spec/plan pair stops being the smallest safe dispatch unit.
30	
31	## Context
32	
33	A brief and a spec answer different questions. A brief holds a shared outcome,
34	its decomposition, and work that may be deferred. A spec is the complete
35	contract for one independently shippable slice. Its plan describes how that
36	contract will be built and verified.
37	
38	The current workspace model weakens this distinction. `capture-work` creates no
39	spec artifact and instead asks for comments detailed enough that a later session
40	can reconstruct one. Other workflow paths register tracker collections or brief
41	prose before a shippable contract exists. Two sessions can therefore interpret
42	the same queue differently because routing depends on prose, nearby comments, or
43	context retained from an earlier conversation.
44	
45	Forcing the opposite extreme is also wrong. A valid brief may sit for weeks or
46	months before the team chooses a slice. Creating every possible spec and plan as
47	soon as the brief is accepted produces speculative delivery contracts that will
48	age before anybody intends to build them.
49	
50	This decision refines ADR-0019 part 2. A feature does not automatically become an
51	immediately executable brief. A brief may persist as the repo-local planning
52	envelope; selected delivery materializes below it. ADR-0019 otherwise remains
53	Accepted. ADR-0009's brief layer and plan-owned LLD, ADR-0033's open `Level`
54	model, and ADR-0051's TOML/main-branch decisions remain in force.
55	
56	## Decision
57	
58	**We will allow accepted briefs to persist without specs, materialize only
59	selected delivery slices as spec/plan pairs, and use `workspace.toml` as a
60	deterministic index over those artifacts rather than as a requirements store.**
61	
62	- **D1:** An accepted brief may remain Ready with no specs, queued specs, or
63	  shipped specs, and may stay Ready indefinitely.
64	- **D2:** Only slices the user confirms as independently shippable are
65	  materialized, and `new-spec` creates a `spec.md` and `plan.md` pair for each.
66	- **D3:** Each derived spec records its `Brief:` back-link and source
67	  provenance, and that value must match the brief path recorded in the workspace
68	  source index.
69	- **D4:** Structured work entries are added only after the spec and plan files
70	  exist.
71	- **D5:** `work-loop` reads the spec and plan and never reconstructs
72	  requirements from workspace comments.
73	- **D6:** Routing may use only parsed entry fields, file existence,
74	  machine-readable artifact status, and explicit hard dependencies; comment
75	  text, list order, nearby prose, and prior-session memory have no routing
76	  meaning.
77	- **D7:** A dispatchable entry must reference an existing `spec.md` with a
78	  sibling `plan.md`.
79	- **D8:** Deferred work stays in the brief and must not be stored only in a
80	  comment.
81	- **D9:** Missing artifacts, mismatched links, malformed entries, duplicate
82	  lifecycle membership, and impossible transitions are reconciliation failures,
83	  and readers fail closed rather than falling back to comments.
84	
85	A brief follows this lifecycle:
86	
87	- **Draft:** its load-bearing fields or acceptance are incomplete.
88	- **Ready:** it is accepted and has no active child spec. It may have no specs,
89	  queued specs, or shipped specs, and may remain Ready indefinitely.
90	- **Executing:** at least one derived spec is active.
91	- **Shipped:** the brief is explicitly closed, no in-scope work remains, and
92	  every materialized child spec is shipped.
93	
94	When delivery is chosen from a Ready brief:
95	
96	1. `receive-brief` presents the proposed cut for the current delivery.
97	2. The user confirms the independently shippable slices.
98	3. `new-spec` creates `spec.md` and `plan.md` for each selected slice.
99	4. Each spec records its `Brief:` back-link and source provenance.
100	5. Structured work entries are added only after the files exist.
101	6. `work-loop` reads the spec and plan; it never reconstructs requirements from
102	   workspace comments.
103	7. After the current batch ships, the brief returns to Ready if scope remains.
104	
105	Deferred work stays in the brief. It does not need a placeholder work entry and
106	must not be stored only in a comment.
107	
108	Routing may use only parsed entry fields, file existence, machine-readable
109	artifact status, and explicit hard dependencies. Comment text, list order,
110	nearby prose, and prior-session memory have no routing meaning.
111	
112	A dispatchable entry must reference an existing `spec.md` with a sibling
113	`plan.md`. A derived spec's `Brief:` value must match the brief path recorded in
114	the workspace source index. Missing artifacts, mismatched links, malformed
115	entries, duplicate lifecycle membership, and impossible transitions are
116	reconciliation failures. Readers fail closed; they never fall back to comments.
117	
118	## Decision drivers
119	
120	- **Deterministic cold starts.** The same files must produce the same ready,
121	  blocked, active, and reconciliation sets in every session.
122	- **One responsibility per artifact.** Briefs hold shared intent and deferred
123	  scope; specs hold delivery contracts; plans hold build strategy; the workspace
124	  indexes and sequences them.
125	- **Safe dispatch.** An agent begins only from a reviewed, existing contract.
126	- **Useful deferral.** Accepting a brief must not force speculative specs.
127	- **Visible drift.** Broken references become findings rather than hidden
128	  inference.
129	
130	## Consequences
131	
132	**Positive:**
133	
134	- A Ready brief remains useful even when no delivery work has been selected.
135	- Work cannot become executable until its spec and plan exist.
136	- Deleting or rewriting comments cannot change routing.
137	- `workspace-status` can report missing files and inconsistent provenance
138	  mechanically.
139	- A completed delivery batch does not falsely close a brief that still has
140	  deferred scope.
141	
142	**Negative:**
143	
144	- Starting work from a brief takes an extra, explicit materialization step.
145	- The brief relationship appears in both spec metadata and the workspace index;
146	  readers must reconcile mismatches.
147	- Ready briefs can age. Tracker-origin sources may need a reviewed refresh before
148	  a deferred slice is materialized.
149	- Existing comment-rich queue entries cannot remain dispatchable and will need
150	  migration or classification as non-dispatchable captures.
151	- `brief_queue` needs a structured Shipped state to retain completed history.
152	
153	**Revisit if:** adopters need briefs themselves to be executable, or a spec/plan
154	pair stops being the smallest safe dispatch unit.
155	
156	## Confirmation
157	
158	- **Mode:** architecture fitness test
159	- **Signal:** every dispatchable entry resolves to `spec.md` and sibling
160	  `plan.md`; brief links agree; changing comments leaves routing unchanged; two
161	  reads of the same tree return identical lifecycle and reconciliation sets; a
162	  Ready brief with no specs remains valid and non-dispatchable.
163	- **Owner:** maintainers
164	
165	## Alternatives considered
166	
167	**Dispatch briefs directly.** `work-loop` could infer a spec from the brief when
168	execution starts. Rejected because a multi-spec brief does not identify one
169	complete delivery contract, and inference would vary across sessions.
170	
171	**Create all specs when a brief becomes Ready.** This makes every planned slice
172	immediately indexable. Rejected because it turns deferred work into speculative
173	contracts that drift before implementation.
174	
175	**Keep requirements in workspace comments.** This is cheap at capture time and
176	keeps everything in one file. Rejected because comments are untyped,
177	unvalidated, and not a stable contract boundary.
178	
179	**Store full requirements as structured TOML.** This could make workspace-only
180	dispatch deterministic. Rejected because it duplicates briefs and specs,
181	creates a second requirements schema, and forces workspace changes whenever
182	requirements change.
183	
184	## References
185	
186	- [`docs/architecture/work-intake-and-artifact-routing.md`](../architecture/work-intake-and-artifact-routing.md)
187	- [ADR-0009](0009-product-brief-layer-and-plan-owned-lld.md)
188	- [ADR-0019](0019-product-intent-ontology-and-brief-projection.md)
189	- [ADR-0033](0033-intent-level-open-recognized-set-decoupled-from-scale.md)
190	- [ADR-0051](0051-workspace-toml-toml-format-and-main-branch-coordination.md)

reconciliation failures. Readers fail closed; they never fall back to comments.

- **Deterministic cold starts.** The same files must produce the same ready,
  blocked, active, and reconciliation sets in every session.
- **One responsibility per artifact.** Briefs hold shared intent and deferred
  scope; specs hold delivery contracts; plans hold build strategy; the workspace
  indexes and sequences them.
- **Safe dispatch.** An agent begins only from a reviewed, existing contract.
- **Useful deferral.** Accepting a brief must not force speculative specs.
- **Visible drift.** Broken references become findings rather than hidden
  inference.

## Consequences

**Positive:**

- A Ready brief remains useful even when no delivery work has been selected.
- Work cannot become executable until its spec and plan exist.
- Deleting or rewriting comments cannot change routing.
- `workspace-status` can report missing files and inconsistent provenance
  mechanically.
- A completed delivery batch does not falsely close a brief that still has
  deferred scope.

**Negative:**

- Starting work from a brief takes an extra, explicit materialization step.
- The brief relationship appears in both spec metadata and the workspace index;
  readers must reconcile mismatches.
- Ready briefs can age. Tracker-origin sources may need a reviewed refresh before
  a deferred slice is materialized.
- Existing comment-rich queue entries cannot remain dispatchable and will need
  migration or classification as non-dispatchable captures.
- `brief_queue` needs a structured Shipped state to retain completed history.

**Revisit if:** adopters need briefs themselves to be executable, or a spec/plan
pair stops being the smallest safe dispatch unit.

## Confirmation

- **Mode:** architecture fitness test
- **Signal:** every dispatchable entry resolves to `spec.md` and sibling
  `plan.md`; brief links agree; changing comments leaves routing unchanged; two
  reads of the same tree return identical lifecycle and reconciliation sets; a
  Ready brief with no specs remains valid and non-dispatchable.
- **Owner:** maintainers

## Alternatives considered

**Dispatch briefs directly.** `work-loop` could infer a spec from the brief when
execution starts. Rejected because a multi-spec brief does not identify one
complete delivery contract, and inference would vary across sessions.

**Create all specs when a brief becomes Ready.** This makes every planned slice
immediately indexable. Rejected because it turns deferred work into speculative
contracts that drift before implementation.

**Keep requirements in workspace comments.** This is cheap at capture time and
keeps everything in one file. Rejected because comments are untyped,
unvalidated, and not a stable contract boundary.

**Store full requirements as structured TOML.** This could make workspace-only
dispatch deterministic. Rejected because it duplicates briefs and specs,
creates a second requirements schema, and forces workspace changes whenever
requirements change.

## References

- [`docs/architecture/work-intake-and-artifact-routing.md`](../architecture/work-intake-and-artifact-routing.md)
- [ADR-0009](0009-product-brief-layer-and-plan-owned-lld.md)
- [ADR-0019](0019-product-intent-ontology-and-brief-projection.md)
- [ADR-0033](0033-intent-level-open-recognized-set-decoupled-from-scale.md)
- [ADR-0051](0051-workspace-toml-toml-format-and-main-branch-coordination.md)

| One independently shippable change in one repository | Feature intent → spec |

57	to find, sequence, display, and reconcile them.

60	
61	**We will make `work-intake` the standalone core entry point, place the minimal
62	intent contract in that shared layer, and treat `workspace.toml` as a
63	deterministic index over canonical artifacts rather than as a requirements
64	store.**

67	  four adopter intents: start or do this, remember this for later, where are we,
68	  and refresh this from the source.

71	- **D3:** The router is part of core and depends on no optional discovery,
72	  prioritization, or shaping pack.

75	  semantics.

79	  `Level`, `Outcome`, `Opportunity`, `Assumptions`, and `Source`, and whose
80	  shared lifecycle is Draft, Accepted, Fulfilled, or Superseded.

85	  `kind`, `source`, `summary`, and `needs`.

87	  acceptance decisions, and closure evidence, while `workspace.toml` owns local
88	  lifecycle membership and the minimal routing and display index.

91	  processor meaning.

93	  links, duplicate membership, unknown kinds, malformed entries, unresolved

104	
105	- **Start or do this:** classify normalized content, materialize the canonical
106	  artifact, register it, and invoke the processor that owns the next step.
107	- **Remember this for later:** materialize a Draft canonical artifact, register
108	  non-executable lifecycle state, and stop.

116	artifacts by reference, but they cannot redefine their shared fields, identity,

150	consequence without changing its TOML format or main-branch coordination
151	decision.

154	provenance, and dependencies it names. Missing artifacts or plans, unsafe paths,
155	mismatched brief/spec links, duplicate membership, unknown kinds, malformed

191	- Changing comments, summaries, ordering, or tracker labels cannot change

executable without materializing and approving its contract.

## Decision drivers

- **Standalone adoption:** core intake must work when no optional product or
  shaping pack is installed.
- **Deterministic cold starts:** the same repository files must produce the same

- **Safe execution:** no agent may begin implementation from comments, missing

- **Relocatable but portable output:** adopters may move intent output through

- **Visible drift:** mismatches must become findings rather than implicit repair

**Positive:**

1	# ADR-0079: Executable plugin branch — dedicated publisher identity
2	
3	- **Status:** Accepted
4	- **Date:** 2026-08-10
5	- **Areas:** distribution, security, ci
6	- **Reversibility:** high
7	- **Decision-makers:** eugenelim
8	- **Consulted:** security-reviewer, adversarial-reviewer
9	- **Supersedes:** none
10	- **Supersedes in part:** none
11	- **Superseded by:** none
12	- **Superseded in part:** none
13	- **Related:** ADR-0072
14	
15	## Decision summary
16	
17	- **Decision:** Only a dedicated, repository-scoped GitHub App may update
18	  `claude-plugins-dist`.
19	- **Because:** A generic Actions-app bypass identifies the platform actor, not
20	  the reviewed publisher workflow.
21	- **Applies to:** Claude-plugin dist publication and its CI authentication
22	  boundary.
23	- **Tradeoff accepted:** Publishing gains an owner-approved environment step
24	  and an operational app credential.
25	- **Revisit if:** GitHub offers workflow-scoped ruleset bypass or the
26	  marketplace moves to immutable commit SHAs.
27	
28	## Context
29	
30	`claude-plugins-dist` serves executable plugin code from a mutable branch.
31	Existing force-push and deletion restrictions protect history but do not stop an
32	ordinary fast-forward push from replacing hook bodies.
33	
34	The current publisher uses `GITHUB_TOKEN` with `contents: write`. That token
35	represents GitHub's repository Actions app. Allowing that app through a branch
36	ruleset would permit every workflow with an equivalent token to update the
37	executable branch.
38	
39	GitHub rulesets can restrict updates to named bypass actors, protected
40	environments can hold credentials until approval, and GitHub Apps provide
41	short-lived installation tokens with repository-scoped permissions.
42	
43	## Decision
44	
45	We will make a dedicated publisher GitHub App the sole bypass actor for an
46	exact-branch ruleset protecting `refs/heads/claude-plugins-dist`.
47	
48	- **D1:** A dedicated publisher GitHub App is the sole bypass actor for an
49	  exact-branch ruleset protecting `refs/heads/claude-plugins-dist`.
50	- **D2:** That app is installed only on this repository and holds Contents
51	  read/write with no other write permission.
52	- **D3:** The app's app ID and private key live only in the
53	  `claude-plugin-publish` environment, which accepts `main`, requires owner
54	  approval, and disallows protection-rule bypass.
55	- **D4:** The publishing workflow's ordinary `GITHUB_TOKEN` is read-only, and
56	  checkout persists no credential.
57	- **D5:** Every external action in that workflow is pinned to a full commit SHA.
58	- **D6:** The short-lived app token is minted only after environment approval and
59	  is supplied only to the final publisher step, through a non-logged subprocess
60	  environment.
61	- **D7:** Desired settings and sanitized live evidence are independently
62	  represented and checked by a pure-stdlib repository lint.
63	
64	The app is installed only on this repository and has Contents read/write with
65	no other write permission. Its app ID and private key live only in the
66	`claude-plugin-publish` environment, which accepts `main`, requires owner
67	approval, and disallows protection-rule bypass.
68	
69	The workflow's ordinary `GITHUB_TOKEN` is read-only. Checkout persists no
70	credential. Every external action is pinned to a full commit SHA. A short-lived
71	app token is minted after environment approval and supplied only to the final
72	publisher step through a non-logged subprocess environment.
73	
74	Desired settings and sanitized live evidence are independently represented and
75	checked by a pure-stdlib repository lint.
76	
77	## Decision drivers
78	
79	- Prevent direct or unrelated-workflow updates to executable plugin content.
80	- Preserve the existing machine-generated dist branch and marketplace topology.
81	- Avoid user-bound, long-lived credentials.
82	- Make configuration drift and rollout evidence mechanically reviewable.
83	
84	## Consequences
85	
86	**Positive:**
87

# ADR-0079: Executable plugin branch — dedicated publisher identity

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-08-10
- **Areas:** distribution, security, ci
- **Reversibility:** high
- **Decision-makers:** eugenelim
- **Consulted:** security-reviewer, adversarial-reviewer
- **Supersedes:** none
- **Supersedes in part:** none
- **Superseded by:** none
- **Superseded in part:** none
- **Related:** ADR-0072

## Decision summary

- **Decision:** Only a dedicated, repository-scoped GitHub App may update
  `claude-plugins-dist`.
- **Because:** A generic Actions-app bypass identifies the platform actor, not
  the reviewed publisher workflow.
- **Applies to:** Claude-plugin dist publication and its CI authentication
  boundary.
- **Tradeoff accepted:** Publishing gains an owner-approved environment step
  and an operational app credential.
- **Revisit if:** GitHub offers workflow-scoped ruleset bypass or the
  marketplace moves to immutable commit SHAs.

## Context

`claude-plugins-dist` serves executable plugin code from a mutable branch.
Existing force-push and deletion restrictions protect history but do not stop an
ordinary fast-forward push from replacing hook bodies.

The current publisher uses `GITHUB_TOKEN` with `contents: write`. That token
represents GitHub's repository Actions app. Allowing that app through a branch
ruleset would permit every workflow with an equivalent token to update the
executable branch.

GitHub rulesets can restrict updates to named bypass actors, protected
environments can hold credentials until approval, and GitHub Apps provide
short-lived installation tokens with repository-scoped permissions.

## Decision

We will make a dedicated publisher GitHub App the sole bypass actor for an
exact-branch ruleset protecting `refs/heads/claude-plugins-dist`.

- **D1:** A dedicated publisher GitHub App is the sole bypass actor for an
  exact-branch ruleset protecting `refs/heads/claude-plugins-dist`.
- **D2:** That app is installed only on this repository and holds Contents
  read/write with no other write permission.
- **D3:** The app's app ID and private key live only in the
  `claude-plugin-publish` environment, which accepts `main`, requires owner
  approval, and disallows protection-rule bypass.
- **D4:** The publishing workflow's ordinary `GITHUB_TOKEN` is read-only, and
  checkout persists no credential.
- **D5:** Every external action in that workflow is pinned to a full commit SHA.
- **D6:** The short-lived app token is minted only after environment approval and
  is supplied only to the final publisher step, through a non-logged subprocess
  environment.
- **D7:** Desired settings and sanitized live evidence are independently
  represented and checked by a pure-stdlib repository lint.

The app is installed only on this repository and has Contents read/write with
no other write permission. Its app ID and private key live only in the
`claude-plugin-publish` environment, which accepts `main`, requires owner
approval, and disallows protection-rule bypass.

The workflow's ordinary `GITHUB_TOKEN` is read-only. Checkout persists no
credential. Every external action is pinned to a full commit SHA. A short-lived
app token is minted after environment approval and supplied only to the final
publisher step through a non-logged subprocess environment.

Desired settings and sanitized live evidence are independently represented and
checked by a pure-stdlib repository lint.

## Decision drivers

- Prevent direct or unrelated-workflow updates to executable plugin content.
- Preserve the existing machine-generated dist branch and marketplace topology.
- Avoid user-bound, long-lived credentials.
- Make configuration drift and rollout evidence mechanically reviewable.

## Consequences

**Positive:**

- Ordinary writers and unrelated workflows cannot update the executable branch.
- Each publication has an explicit approval and audit event.
- Publisher credentials are short-lived and repository-scoped.
- The existing branch name and plugin source shape remain unchanged.

**Negative:**

- The repository owner must create and maintain a GitHub App, environment, and
  ruleset.
- Every publication requires environment approval.
- The app credential remains high-value during an approved publishing job.
- The mutable ref still lacks adopter-verifiable content hashes.

**Revisit if:** GitHub offers workflow-scoped ruleset bypass or the marketplace
moves to immutable commit SHAs.

## Confirmation

- **Mode:** architecture fitness test + periodic audit
- **Signal:** workflow construction lint, desired-state/evidence comparison,
  ordinary-identity canary rejection, publisher-app canary acceptance, and
  sanitized live settings snapshots
- **Owner:** repository owner

## Alternatives considered

- **Bypass the generic GitHub Actions app** — rejected against *prevent direct or
  unrelated-workflow updates to executable plugin content*: all workflow
  `GITHUB_TOKEN`s represent that app, so it cannot distinguish one workflow.
- **Require pull requests on the generated dist branch** — rejected against
  *preserve the existing machine-generated dist branch and marketplace topology*:
  it replaces deterministic machine publication with a second review/merge
  lifecycle.
- **Use a personal token or deploy key** — rejected against *avoid user-bound,
  long-lived credentials*: it is long-lived or user-bound and has a weaker
  approval boundary.
- **Pin marketplace entries to immutable SHAs** — deferred against *preserve the
  existing machine-generated dist branch and marketplace topology*: a desirable
  follow-on, but the current marketplace/dist publishing cycle cannot know its
  own resulting commit before publication without changing topology.

## References

- [GitHub: available rules for rulesets](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-rulesets/available-rules-for-rulesets)
- [GitHub: deployments and environments](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/deployments-and-environments)
- [GitHub: `GITHUB_TOKEN`](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/github_token)
- [GitHub: `actions/create-github-app-token`](https://github.com/actions/create-github-app-token/blob/main/README.md)

## Errata

Corrections below are Approver-signed. The body above is preserved unchanged;
errata supersede where noted. This ADR is Accepted → Frozen
(`docs/CONVENTIONS.md`). (Approver: eugenelim, 2026-08-12.)

- **2026-08-12 — the control is live; *Confirmation* is satisfied.** Every signal
  the *Confirmation* section names has been exercised. The publisher App is
  installed on this repository only, with Contents read/write as its sole write
  permission. The `claude-plugin-publish` environment admits `main` only,
  requires one reviewer, prevents self-review, and disallows admin bypass. An
  active ruleset targets exactly `refs/heads/claude-plugins-dist`, restricting
  updates and deletions and blocking force pushes, with the App as its only
  always-bypass actor. On a canary ref, an ordinary owner push was rejected
  (`GH013 … push declined due to repository rule violations`) and the same commit
  pushed with an App installation token was accepted (`Bypassed rule
  violations …`); the canary was then removed with the App identity and the
  ruleset retargeted, so the live branch was never a negative probe. The
  sanitized snapshot is committed at
  `docs/specs/claude-plugin-hook-parity/publish-control-evidence.json`.

- **2026-08-12 — the decision needed an ordering rule it did not state.** This
  ADR specified the end state but not the identity to hold *until* the App
  exists. The token-minting step consequently merged ahead of its credentials
  and every push to `main` failed at
  `[@octokit/auth-app] appId option is required` for eight consecutive commits,
  while the construction tests stayed green because they asserted the end-state
  workflow shape without asking whether the credentials it named existed.
  `docs/specs/claude-plugin-hook-parity` AC36 closes this: the workflow's
  identity must match provisioning state, read offline from whether the evidence
  file exists, and both directions fail closed — an App-token workflow without
  evidence is refused, and so is the interim publisher once evidence lands. The
  decision is unchanged; it is now sequenced.

- **2026-08-12 — `prevent_self_review` is disabled; the gate was unsatisfiable.**
  The *Decision* above specifies an environment that "requires owner approval"
  together with self-review prevention. On a repository where one person merges
  every change, that person is always the deployment's triggering actor, so
  GitHub withholds the approval control from the only account that holds it —
  and with `can_admins_bypass` false there is no override. The first real
  publication after rollout sat in `waiting` with
  `current_user_can_approve: false` and **could not be approved by anyone**.

  The canary probes did not catch this because they minted an App token directly
  rather than routing through the environment, so the approval path was never
  exercised end to end until a live publish.

  `prevent_self_review` is therefore now `false`. The reviewer requirement
  stands: every publication still waits for a human to release it deliberately,
  and `can_admins_bypass` stays `false` so the gate cannot be stepped around.
  What is lost is the second pair of eyes, which a single-maintainer repository
  could never actually supply. Restoring `true` requires a second trusted
  reviewer account, and would otherwise reintroduce the deadlock.

- **2026-08-12 — no internal identifier is recorded.** The *Confirmation*
  signal "sanitized live settings snapshots" is narrowed: the evidence artifact
  carries no App, installation, ruleset, account, or node ID. The three-way
  identity agreement between the ruleset bypass actor, the App installation, and
  the environment's App ID variable is computed against live state at capture
  time and committed as a single asserted boolean, and the repository lint walks
  the artifact to refuse any forbidden identifier key. Recorded as AC36
  clause 6. This strengthens "sanitized" rather than relaxing it.

   same-principal destination poisoning.

  operator-typed; architecture and product specifications describe destination
  validation only as defense in depth; no open workspace item claims a
  same-principal destination enforcer
- **Owner:** credential-brokers maintainers

## Alternatives considered

- **Another Python package or virtual environment** — rejected against *avoid
  maintaining an additional package that changes packaging without changing
  authority*: it remains owned and bypassable by the agent principal.
- **A root-owned or signed policy with the current verifier** — rejected against
  *do not claim a security boundary the supported installation cannot provide*: a
  user-writable or bypassable verifier cannot enforce that policy.
- **A browser extension, privileged helper, or local service** — rejected against
  *do not claim a security boundary the supported installation cannot provide*:
  technically viable, but outside the supported installation envelope.
- **Implement protocol-backed authorization now** — rejected against *keep future
  protocol-backed authentication possible without pretending it solves generic
  cookie capture*: there is no concrete consumer, issuer contract, client
  registration, credential type, or migration path.
- **Remove generic headed capture** — rejected against *preserve generic
  SSO-cookie compatibility*: explicit operator capture remains a useful
  compatibility workflow when its limitation is understood.

## References

- [RFC-0084](../rfc/0084-sso-destination-trust-boundary.md)
- [Credential architecture](../architecture/credentials.md)
- [RFC 8252: OAuth 2.0 for Native Apps](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8252.html)
- [RFC 8628: OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8628.html)

1	# ADR-0083: Extend the SAST/SCA gate to npm with `npm audit` + a reasoned allowlist
2	
3	- **Status:** Accepted
4	- **Date:** 2026-08-16
5	- **Areas:** security, ci
6	- **Reversibility:** high
7	- **Decision-makers:** eugenelim
8	- **Supersedes:** none
9	- **Supersedes in part:** none
10	- **Superseded by:** none
11	- **Superseded in part:** none
12	- **Related:** extends ADR-0017 (Bandit + pip-audit + Semgrep as the repo's SAST/SCA gate)
13	  to a second ecosystem
14	
15	## Context
16	
17	ADR-0017 adopted Bandit + pip-audit + Semgrep and named the result the repo's
18	"SAST/SCA gate". The SCA half is `pip-audit`, and it is thorough: every
19	third-party pin in `tools/requirements.txt`, every `packs/**/requirements.txt`,
20	both PEP 517 build-system tables, the SAST tooling's own requirements, and
21	`credbroker`'s optional `[crypto]` extra.
22	
23	It audits no JavaScript, because there was none in the tree when ADR-0017 was
24	written. There is now:
25	
26	- `web/` — the marketing site, approved by RFC-0061, first Node toolchain in the
27	  repo.
28	- `docs-site/` — the Starlight docs site.
29	
30	Both commit a `package-lock.json`, and both ship their resolved trees into built
31	output. `spec/docs-site-design-refresh` (AC9) made this materially worse in a way
32	worth naming: it replaced mermaid's runtime CDN `<script>` with a bundled
33	`mermaid@11.16.1` dependency. That was the right call for the CDN-call boundary
34	it was solving, and it vendored mermaid's entire transitive tree into shipped
35	output. That spec recorded the consequence honestly as a deferral
36	(`docs-site-npm-sca-gap`) rather than pretending it was covered.
37	
38	The gap was not theoretical. At the time this ADR was written, both lockfiles
39	carried two unremediated **high**-severity advisories (`js-yaml`
40	GHSA-5p4m-2wfm-xmqj, `nanoid` GHSA-2v37-7h3g-55p8) and `web/` additionally
41	carried a moderate `postcss` advisory. Nothing in the repo would have said so.
42	That is precisely the class of finding ADR-0017 § Context names as its reason
43	for existing: the org's Snyk scan reports it, and the maintainer cannot see that
44	scan's output.
45	
46	## Decision
47	
48	**Add `npm audit` as a fourth scanner on the existing `make sast` gate, invoked
49	through a thin stdlib wrapper (`tools/audit-npm.py`) that carries a reasoned
50	advisory allowlist.**
51	
52	- **D1:** `npm audit` runs as a fourth scanner on the existing `make sast` gate,
53	  invoked through a stdlib-only wrapper, not as a new workflow or a job outside
54	  `tools/lint-ci-parity.py`'s `WORKFLOW_SCOPE`.
55	- **D2:** Both lockfiles are listed in the Makefile's `SAST_CONFIG`, so a PR whose
56	  only changed file is a lockfile does not set `SKIP_SAST=1`.
57	- **D3:** Advisory suppressions live in a reasoned allowlist, and every entry
58	  carries `id`, a non-blank `reason`, and a non-blank `unblocked_when`; a missing
59	  or blank field is a tool error, never a silent pass.
60	- **D4:** A clean verdict is reachable only from a parsed payload carrying
61	  `auditReportVersion`; npm absent, unparseable output, an `error` key, an
62	  unrecognised schema, or zero lockfiles discovered all exit 2 as a tool error.
63	- **D5:** The blocking threshold is `moderate` and above; `low` and `info` stay
64	  ungated.
65	- **D6:** Lockfiles are discovered by walking the tree, never listed, so a third
66	  npm project cannot be added without the gate noticing.
67	- **D7:** The gate audits a known-vulnerable canary lockfile first; if the
68	  endpoint does not report that advisory, the run is a tool error rather than a
69	  pass.
70	
71	### Why a leg on `make sast` rather than a new workflow
72	
73	`make sast` is chained into `make build-check`, which is what `build-check.yml`
74	runs — and `build-check.yml` is the **one** workflow inside
75	`tools/lint-ci-parity.py`'s `WORKFLOW_SCOPE`. A gate added there is locally
76	reproducible and drift-checked by construction.
77	
78	The alternatives all forfeit that. A job in `ci-security.yml` or a new workflow
79	file lands outside parity scope, which is the exact defect
80	`spec/local-gate-ci-parity` was written to close: a CI step with no local
81	counterpart and nothing detecting the divergence. Putting npm SCA anywhere other
82	than the gate already named "SCA" would also leave a reader reconciling two
83	coverage stories by hand.
84	
85	One consequence has to be wired deliberately: **both lockfiles are added to the
86	Makefile's `SAST_CONFIG`.** `build-check.yml` computes SAST relevance from
87	`SAST_DIRS` + `SAST_CONFIG` against the PR's changed files and sets
88	`SKIP_SAST=1` when nothing matches. Neither `docs-site/` nor `web/` is under
89	`SAST_DIRS`, so without this a dependency-bump PR — a diff whose only changed
90	file is a lockfile — would skip the one gate written to check it.
91	
92	### Why `npm audit` rather than Dependabot or Snyk Open Source
93	
94	| Option | Blocks a merge? | Cost | Verdict |
95	|---|---|---|---|
96	| **`npm audit`** | Yes — it is a gate | Zero: ships with npm, already on every runner and contributor machine | **Chosen** |
97	| Dependabot | No — it opens bump PRs | Free, but changes team PR volume and review workload | Deferred (`npm-dependabot-wiring`); complementary, not a substitute |
98	| Snyk Open Source | Yes | Needs an account and a token in CI | Rejected: ADR-0017 already rejected tool choices requiring org-scan access the maintainer does not have |
99	
100	Dependabot and `npm audit` answer different questions — "should we bump?" versus
101	"may this merge?" — so choosing the gate first is not a rejection of Dependabot,
102	only an ordering. Adopting it remains open as a backlog item, deliberately left
103	to the repo owner because it changes how much review the team absorbs per week.
104	
105	### Why a wrapper rather than two `npm audit` lines in the recipe
106	
107	`npm audit` has **no per-advisory ignore**. Its only lever is `--audit-level`,
108	which is repo-wide and coarse: the escape hatch for a single unfixable
109	transitive advisory is to stop gating an entire severity band.
110	
111	That matters here specifically because suppressions are the observed steady state
112	of this control in this repo, not a hypothesis. The sibling `pip-audit` leg runs
113	today with four live `--ignore-vuln` entries (Semgrep's hard-pinned `mcp` and
114	`click` transitive CVEs), each carrying a written diagnosis and an unblock
115	condition. A gate shipped without an escape hatch would wedge every merge the
116	first time a no-fix-available advisory lands — and the hatch would then be
117	designed under exactly the pressure that produces a bad one.
118	
119	So `tools/npm-audit-allowlist.toml` ships **empty**, and every entry must carry
120	`id`, a non-blank `reason`, and a non-blank `unblocked_when`. A missing or blank
121	field is a tool error, not a silent pass: an allowlist that decays into an
122	undocumented mute list is worse than no allowlist.
123	
124	### Why the verdict is read from the payload, not the exit code
125	
126	`npm audit` exits non-zero for *both* "found advisories" and "could not reach the
127	registry". Reading the exit code alone would make a network outage, a proxy
128	returning an HTML error page, or a corporate MITM indistinguishable from a clean
129	tree — a gate that fails **open** exactly when the environment is degraded.
130	
131	So a "clean" verdict is reachable only from a parsed payload carrying
132	`auditReportVersion`. Everything else — npm absent, unparseable output, an
133	`error` key, an unrecognised schema, or zero lockfiles discovered — exits 2, the
134	distinct tool-error code. `tools/test-audit-npm.py` pins those paths against
135	fixtures, because a live run against a healthy registry never reaches them.
136	
137	### Threshold and scope
138	
139	Blocking at **`moderate`** and above. The first draft of this decision said
140	`high`, on the reasoning that it matched Bandit's medium/medium tuning and that
141	tightening could come later. Implementation reversed it on evidence: remediating
142	`web/`'s moderate `postcss` advisory left both lockfiles clean at `moderate`, so
143	the bar could be raised for free. A threshold is cheapest to raise while you are
144	already above it; deferring guarantees the tightening lands on a day when
145	something is failing it. `low` and `info` stay ungated.
146	
147	Lockfiles are **discovered** by walking the tree, not listed, so a third npm
148	project cannot be added without the gate noticing.
149	
150	### Why a canary probe — reading the payload is not sufficient
151	
152	The rule above ("clean requires `auditReportVersion`") is necessary and **not
153	sufficient**, which we measured rather than argued.
154	
155	Pointed at a local stub that answers the bulk-advisory endpoint with HTTP 200
156	and an empty body, `npm audit` returns:
157	
158	```json
159	{ "auditReportVersion": 2, "vulnerabilities": {},
160	  "metadata": { "dependencies": { "total": 573, "...": "..." } } }
161	```
162	
163	No `error` key. A correct report version. A full and entirely plausible
164	dependency count — because **npm computes `metadata.dependencies` locally from
165	the lockfile and never receives it from the registry.** The payload is
166	byte-identical to a genuinely clean audit. No inspection of it can tell the two
167	apart, which also rules out the obvious cross-check (comparing the audited
168	dependency count against the lockfile's package count); that number is local
169	knowledge and stays correct while the advisory data is missing entirely.
170	
171	The threat is mundane: an internal npm mirror — Artifactory, Nexus, Verdaccio —
172	whose advisory endpoint is unimplemented, misconfigured, or silently degraded.
173	ADR-0017 § Context establishes that this repo lives alongside an org-managed
174	scanning estate, so a non-default registry is a realistic configuration rather
175	than a hypothetical one.
176	
177	So the gate audits a **canary** first: a throwaway lockfile pinning
178	`lodash@4.17.11`, whose critical prototype-pollution advisory
179	(GHSA-jf85-cpcp-j695) has been published for years. If the endpoint does not
180	report it, the endpoint is not reporting anything, and the run is a tool error
181	rather than a pass.
182	
183	This is the same argument the `sast` recipe already makes for
184	`tools/test-semgrep-argv-boundary.py`: a scan that is silent when it works and
185	silent when it has been broken into a no-op cannot tell you which one happened,
186	so something known-positive has to be run through it.
187	
188	## Consequences
189	
190	**Positive:**
191	- The gate's name and its coverage now agree. Both dependency ecosystems in the
192	  tree are scanned by the same `make sast` invocation, locally and in CI.
193	- Three real advisories were found and fixed on arrival — all transitive patch
194	  bumps that left both `package.json` files untouched.
195	- The escape hatch exists before it is needed, so the first suppression is a
196	  reviewed diff with a written unblock condition rather than an emergency
197	  `--audit-level` downgrade.
198	- No new dependency: `npm` is already required to build either site, and the
199	  wrapper is pure stdlib, preserving ADR-0017's dev/CI-only-tooling posture.
200	
201	**Negative:**
202	- `make sast` gains another network-bound leg. ADR-0017 already accepted this
203	  trade for Semgrep's registry fetches and pip-audit's index resolution;
204	  `SKIP_SAST=1` remains the documented offline path.
205	- The advisory database moves independently of the repo, so a previously green
206	  gate can redden with no diff. Identical to the `pip-audit` and Semgrep legs;
207	  the allowlist is the response.
208	- `npm` becomes a hard requirement of `make sast` on a machine that previously
209	  needed only Python. Guarded explicitly with an install hint rather than
210	  skipped silently — a skipped SCA leg that still prints green is the failure
211	  mode this whole gate exists to avoid.
212	
213	**Neutral / to revisit:**
214	- **Tightening to `low`.** Not taken. `moderate` is the floor that maps most
215	  nearly onto Bandit's `medium`; going lower would gate advisory noise that the
216	  Python half of the same gate deliberately ignores.
217	- **The canary pin is a maintenance item.** If GHSA-jf85-cpcp-j695 is ever
218	  withdrawn, the probe goes silent and the gate wedges closed — loudly, with an
219	  error naming the fix (repin the canary). Failing closed on a withdrawn
220	  advisory is the correct direction for the error to point, but it is a real
221	  future interrupt and is recorded here so it is diagnosable at a glance.
222	- **The allowlist's `unblocked_when` is prose the gate never reads.** ADR-0017's
223	  `.snyk` policy carries a machine-checked `expires`; mirroring that here would
224	  stop a suppression rotting indefinitely. Deliberately not built while the
225	  allowlist is empty — there is nothing to expire yet.
226	- **Dependabot** (`npm-dependabot-wiring`) — complementary automation, left to
227	  the repo owner.

# ADR-0083: Extend the SAST/SCA gate to npm with `npm audit` + a reasoned allowlist

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-08-16
- **Areas:** security, ci
- **Reversibility:** high
- **Decision-makers:** eugenelim
- **Supersedes:** none
- **Supersedes in part:** none
- **Superseded by:** none
- **Superseded in part:** none
- **Related:** extends ADR-0017 (Bandit + pip-audit + Semgrep as the repo's SAST/SCA gate)
  to a second ecosystem

## Context

ADR-0017 adopted Bandit + pip-audit + Semgrep and named the result the repo's
"SAST/SCA gate". The SCA half is `pip-audit`, and it is thorough: every
third-party pin in `tools/requirements.txt`, every `packs/**/requirements.txt`,
both PEP 517 build-system tables, the SAST tooling's own requirements, and
`credbroker`'s optional `[crypto]` extra.

It audits no JavaScript, because there was none in the tree when ADR-0017 was
written. There is now:

- `web/` — the marketing site, approved by RFC-0061, first Node toolchain in the
  repo.
- `docs-site/` — the Starlight docs site.

Both commit a `package-lock.json`, and both ship their resolved trees into built
output. `spec/docs-site-design-refresh` (AC9) made this materially worse in a way
worth naming: it replaced mermaid's runtime CDN `<script>` with a bundled
`mermaid@11.16.1` dependency. That was the right call for the CDN-call boundary
it was solving, and it vendored mermaid's entire transitive tree into shipped
output. That spec recorded the consequence honestly as a deferral
(`docs-site-npm-sca-gap`) rather than pretending it was covered.

The gap was not theoretical. At the time this ADR was written, both lockfiles
carried two unremediated **high**-severity advisories (`js-yaml`
GHSA-5p4m-2wfm-xmqj, `nanoid` GHSA-2v37-7h3g-55p8) and `web/` additionally
carried a moderate `postcss` advisory. Nothing in the repo would have said so.
That is precisely the class of finding ADR-0017 § Context names as its reason
for existing: the org's Snyk scan reports it, and the maintainer cannot see that
scan's output.

## Decision

**Add `npm audit` as a fourth scanner on the existing `make sast` gate, invoked
through a thin stdlib wrapper (`tools/audit-npm.py`) that carries a reasoned
advisory allowlist.**

- **D1:** `npm audit` runs as a fourth scanner on the existing `make sast` gate,
  invoked through a stdlib-only wrapper, not as a new workflow or a job outside
  `tools/lint-ci-parity.py`'s `WORKFLOW_SCOPE`.
- **D2:** Both lockfiles are listed in the Makefile's `SAST_CONFIG`, so a PR whose
  only changed file is a lockfile does not set `SKIP_SAST=1`.
- **D3:** Advisory suppressions live in a reasoned allowlist, and every entry
  carries `id`, a non-blank `reason`, and a non-blank `unblocked_when`; a missing
  or blank field is a tool error, never a silent pass.
- **D4:** A clean verdict is reachable only from a parsed payload carrying
  `auditReportVersion`; npm absent, unparseable output, an `error` key, an
  unrecognised schema, or zero lockfiles discovered all exit 2 as a tool error.
- **D5:** The blocking threshold is `moderate` and above; `low` and `info` stay
  ungated.
- **D6:** Lockfiles are discovered by walking the tree, never listed, so a third
  npm project cannot be added without the gate noticing.
- **D7:** The gate audits a known-vulnerable canary lockfile first; if the
  endpoint does not report that advisory, the run is a tool error rather than a
  pass.

### Why a leg on `make sast` rather than a new workflow

`make sast` is chained into `make build-check`, which is what `build-check.yml`
runs — and `build-check.yml` is the **one** workflow inside
`tools/lint-ci-parity.py`'s `WORKFLOW_SCOPE`. A gate added there is locally
reproducible and drift-checked by construction.

The alternatives all forfeit that. A job in `ci-security.yml` or a new workflow
file lands outside parity scope, which is the exact defect
`spec/local-gate-ci-parity` was written to close: a CI step with no local
counterpart and nothing detecting the divergence. Putting npm SCA anywhere other
than the gate already named "SCA" would also leave a reader reconciling two
coverage stories by hand.

One consequence has to be wired deliberately: **both lockfiles are added to the
Makefile's `SAST_CONFIG`.** `build-check.yml` computes SAST relevance from
`SAST_DIRS` + `SAST_CONFIG` against the PR's changed files and sets
`SKIP_SAST=1` when nothing matches. Neither `docs-site/` nor `web/` is under
`SAST_DIRS`, so without this a dependency-bump PR — a diff whose only changed
file is a lockfile — would skip the one gate written to check it.

### Why `npm audit` rather than Dependabot or Snyk Open Source

| Option | Blocks a merge? | Cost | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| **`npm audit`** | Yes — it is a gate | Zero: ships with npm, already on every runner and contributor machine | **Chosen** |
| Dependabot | No — it opens bump PRs | Free, but changes team PR volume and review workload | Deferred (`npm-dependabot-wiring`); complementary, not a substitute |
| Snyk Open Source | Yes | Needs an account and a token in CI | Rejected: ADR-0017 already rejected tool choices requiring org-scan access the maintainer does not have |

Dependabot and `npm audit` answer different questions — "should we bump?" versus
"may this merge?" — so choosing the gate first is not a rejection of Dependabot,
only an ordering. Adopting it remains open as a backlog item, deliberately left
to the repo owner because it changes how much review the team absorbs per week.

### Why a wrapper rather than two `npm audit` lines in the recipe

`npm audit` has **no per-advisory ignore**. Its only lever is `--audit-level`,
which is repo-wide and coarse: the escape hatch for a single unfixable
transitive advisory is to stop gating an entire severity band.

That matters here specifically because suppressions are the observed steady state
of this control in this repo, not a hypothesis. The sibling `pip-audit` leg runs
today with four live `--ignore-vuln` entries (Semgrep's hard-pinned `mcp` and
`click` transitive CVEs), each carrying a written diagnosis and an unblock
condition. A gate shipped without an escape hatch would wedge every merge the
first time a no-fix-available advisory lands — and the hatch would then be
designed under exactly the pressure that produces a bad one.

So `tools/npm-audit-allowlist.toml` ships **empty**, and every entry must carry
`id`, a non-blank `reason`, and a non-blank `unblocked_when`. A missing or blank
field is a tool error, not a silent pass: an allowlist that decays into an
undocumented mute list is worse than no allowlist.

### Why the verdict is read from the payload, not the exit code

`npm audit` exits non-zero for *both* "found advisories" and "could not reach the
registry". Reading the exit code alone would make a network outage, a proxy
returning an HTML error page, or a corporate MITM indistinguishable from a clean
tree — a gate that fails **open** exactly when the environment is degraded.

So a "clean" verdict is reachable only from a parsed payload carrying
`auditReportVersion`. Everything else — npm absent, unparseable output, an
`error` key, an unrecognised schema, or zero lockfiles discovered — exits 2, the
distinct tool-error code. `tools/test-audit-npm.py` pins those paths against
fixtures, because a live run against a healthy registry never reaches them.

### Threshold and scope

Blocking at **`moderate`** and above. The first draft of this decision said
`high`, on the reasoning that it matched Bandit's medium/medium tuning and that
tightening could come later. Implementation reversed it on evidence: remediating
`web/`'s moderate `postcss` advisory left both lockfiles clean at `moderate`, so
the bar could be raised for free. A threshold is cheapest to raise while you are
already above it; deferring guarantees the tightening lands on a day when
something is failing it. `low` and `info` stay ungated.

Lockfiles are **discovered** by walking the tree, not listed, so a third npm
project cannot be added without the gate noticing.

### Why a canary probe — reading the payload is not sufficient

The rule above ("clean requires `auditReportVersion`") is necessary and **not
sufficient**, which we measured rather than argued.

Pointed at a local stub that answers the bulk-advisory endpoint with HTTP 200
and an empty body, `npm audit` returns:

```json
{ "auditReportVersion": 2, "vulnerabilities": {},
  "metadata": { "dependencies": { "total": 573, "...": "..." } } }
```

No `error` key. A correct report version. A full and entirely plausible
dependency count — because **npm computes `metadata.dependencies` locally from
the lockfile and never receives it from the registry.** The payload is
byte-identical to a genuinely clean audit. No inspection of it can tell the two
apart, which also rules out the obvious cross-check (comparing the audited
dependency count against the lockfile's package count); that number is local
knowledge and stays correct while the advisory data is missing entirely.

The threat is mundane: an internal npm mirror — Artifactory, Nexus, Verdaccio —
whose advisory endpoint is unimplemented, misconfigured, or silently degraded.
ADR-0017 § Context establishes that this repo lives alongside an org-managed
scanning estate, so a non-default registry is a realistic configuration rather
than a hypothetical one.

So the gate audits a **canary** first: a throwaway lockfile pinning
`lodash@4.17.11`, whose critical prototype-pollution advisory
(GHSA-jf85-cpcp-j695) has been published for years. If the endpoint does not
report it, the endpoint is not reporting anything, and the run is a tool error
rather than a pass.

This is the same argument the `sast` recipe already makes for
`tools/test-semgrep-argv-boundary.py`: a scan that is silent when it works and
silent when it has been broken into a no-op cannot tell you which one happened,
so something known-positive has to be run through it.

## Consequences

**Positive:**
- The gate's name and its coverage now agree. Both dependency ecosystems in the
  tree are scanned by the same `make sast` invocation, locally and in CI.
- Three real advisories were found and fixed on arrival — all transitive patch
  bumps that left both `package.json` files untouched.
- The escape hatch exists before it is needed, so the first suppression is a
  reviewed diff with a written unblock condition rather than an emergency
  `--audit-level` downgrade.
- No new dependency: `npm` is already required to build either site, and the
  wrapper is pure stdlib, preserving ADR-0017's dev/CI-only-tooling posture.

**Negative:**
- `make sast` gains another network-bound leg. ADR-0017 already accepted this
  trade for Semgrep's registry fetches and pip-audit's index resolution;
  `SKIP_SAST=1` remains the documented offline path.
- The advisory database moves independently of the repo, so a previously green
  gate can redden with no diff. Identical to the `pip-audit` and Semgrep legs;
  the allowlist is the response.
- `npm` becomes a hard requirement of `make sast` on a machine that previously
  needed only Python. Guarded explicitly with an install hint rather than
  skipped silently — a skipped SCA leg that still prints green is the failure
  mode this whole gate exists to avoid.

**Neutral / to revisit:**
- **Tightening to `low`.** Not taken. `moderate` is the floor that maps most
  nearly onto Bandit's `medium`; going lower would gate advisory noise that the
  Python half of the same gate deliberately ignores.
- **The canary pin is a maintenance item.** If GHSA-jf85-cpcp-j695 is ever
  withdrawn, the probe goes silent and the gate wedges closed — loudly, with an
  error naming the fix (repin the canary). Failing closed on a withdrawn
  advisory is the correct direction for the error to point, but it is a real
  future interrupt and is recorded here so it is diagnosable at a glance.
- **The allowlist's `unblocked_when` is prose the gate never reads.** ADR-0017's
  `.snyk` policy carries a machine-checked `expires`; mirroring that here would
  stop a suppression rotting indefinitely. Deliberately not built while the
  allowlist is empty — there is nothing to expire yet.
- **Dependabot** (`npm-dependabot-wiring`) — complementary automation, left to
  the repo owner.
- **Machine enforcement of the `allowScripts` install-script invariant**
  (`npm-allowscripts-enforcement`). Both `AGENTS.md` files document it as prose
  and nothing checks it. Deliberately not built here: `web/`'s lockfile already
  carries `playwright/node_modules/fsevents@2.3.2` outside its `allowScripts`
  keys, so the gate would land CI red on arrival. That divergence needs a
  disposition before the check can exist. Note the distinction — SCA scans for
  *known CVEs*; `allowScripts` governs *arbitrary code execution at install
  time*. Neither substitutes for the other.
- **JavaScript SAST** (`sast-javascript-coverage`) remains open. SCA and SAST are
  different lenses; this ADR adds only the first for npm.

**Revisit if:** `npm audit` gains a per-advisory ignore, which would remove the
wrapper's reason to exist (D3); or the canary advisory GHSA-jf85-cpcp-j695 is
withdrawn, which wedges the gate closed until the pin is replaced (D7).
